Duration::total_seconds¶

Back to Duration API Reference

Signature¶

Series Duration::total_nanoseconds() const;
Series Duration::total_microseconds() const;
Series Duration::total_milliseconds() const;
Series Duration::total_seconds() const;
Series Duration::total_minutes() const;
Series Duration::total_hours() const;
Series Duration::total_days() const;
Series Duration::total_weeks() const;

What It Does¶

Converts a Duration’s elapsed magnitude into a plain Series expressed in one chosen unit — the way out of duration-space back into an ordinary numeric Series, e.g. for storing elapsed time in a DataFrame column (recall Duration itself isn’t a ThreadKind payload — see the API reference overview) or feeding it into arithmetic that doesn’t care about the duration/instant distinction.

Every member here is the same underlying value, total_nanoseconds(), just divided by a different constant — total_seconds() divides by 1e9, total_days() by 86'400 * 1e9, and so on. None of them round; a Duration of 90 seconds read through total_minutes() gives 1.5, not 1 or 2.

Parameters¶

None — these are all zero-argument accessors on self.

Returns¶

Series A floating-point Series at self’s shape, in the named unit.

Examples¶

Example 1. The same 90-minute Duration read through three different units.

auto ninety_min = pluss::duration::minutes(90);
std::cout << "seconds=" << pluss::print_series(ninety_min.total_seconds()) << "\n";
std::cout << "minutes=" << pluss::print_series(ninety_min.total_minutes()) << "\n";
std::cout << "hours=" << pluss::print_series(ninety_min.total_hours());

Output¶

seconds=Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=5400.0000
minutes=Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=90.0000
hours=Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=1.5000

Same 90-minute value throughout; only the unit — and therefore the magnitude — changes. total_hours() gives the non-integer 1.5, confirming no unit here rounds.

Example 2. total_days() over an array Duration.

auto ranged = pluss::duration::range(
    pluss::duration::days(0), pluss::duration::days(10), pluss::duration::days(2));
std::cout << pluss::print_series(ranged.total_days());

Output¶

Series(shape=[6], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 2.0000, 4.0000, 6.0000, 8.0000, 10.0000]

The array shape carries through the conversion — one converted value per element, same as every other unit accessor here.

Notes¶

  • total_* never rounds or truncates — the result is always the exact (floating-point) division, which is why total_minutes() on a 90-second Duration correctly reads 1.5, not 1.

  • There are convenience aliases beyond the eight listed in the signature (totalSeconds(), to_seconds(), total_sec(), and similar camelCase/ short-name spellings) — all route to the same underlying total(unit) dispatch and are not separately documented here.

  • To go the other direction (a number back into a Duration), use one of the construction factories, not a total_* method.

See Also¶

  • construction: the inverse direction — building a Duration from a plain count in a chosen unit.

  • abs: magnitude and sign, useful before converting a Duration that might be negative.
